title: Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère
output:
# Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère

**Where to stand**

Stand slightly to the right of the centre of Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère, and step a little closer than feels natural. This is not an arbitrary spot. In 2000, the art historian Malcolm Park staged a physical reconstruction of the scene and showed that its puzzling geometry works only from this position: to the right, and nearer the bar than the gentleman whose reflection appears at the painting's right edge. From dead centre, the mirror seems to lie. From here, the picture starts to make sense.

**The work**

A young woman stands behind a marble bar at the Folies-Bergère, a Parisian nightclub and music hall. She faces you directly, hands resting on the counter. In front of her are bottles of champagne, liqueur and beer, a glass holding two flowers, and a dish of oranges. Behind her stretches the gold frame of an enormous mirror. It runs the full length of this oil on canvas, which is about four and a quarter feet wide. Almost everything else you see, the glittering chandeliers, the crowded balcony and the blur of hats and faces, is reflection.

That mirror is the painting's central compositional choice, and the source of a long argument. From the earliest reviews, critics accused Manet of not understanding perspective. In the mirror, the barmaid's reflection appears far off to the right, leaning towards a top-hatted man. Yet the woman herself stands centred, upright and alone. A preliminary study shows that Manet first placed her off to the right. In the finished canvas he moved her to the centre but deliberately left her reflection where it was. The art historian Jeffrey Meyers sums up the effect: in the mirror she seems engaged with a customer, while face on she is "self-protectively withdrawn and remote."

Park's reconstruction showed that the apparent conversation is an optical trick. The man stands outside the painter's field of vision, to the left, and he is looking away from her. Manet was not making mistakes. He was quietly moving the viewer off-centre, which breaks with the fixed central viewpoint that perspective painting normally assumes.

The woman was a real person, known as Suzon, who worked at the Folies-Bergère in the early 1880s. Manet posed her in his studio. The details around her point to class and commerce. The art historian Larry Ligo argues that Manet habitually used oranges to signal prostitution. T. J. Clark, a leading historian of modern Parisian painting, reads her as both "a salesperson and a commodity," something to be bought along with a drink. In the upper left corner, a pair of small green-slippered feet dangle into the picture. They belong to a trapeze artist performing above the audience, and nobody in the crowd appears to be watching.

Scholars have also linked the mirror to *Las Meninas*, the painting by the seventeenth-century Spanish court painter Diego Velázquez, whom Manet admired, in which a mirror reveals figures standing where the viewer stands. The philosopher Michel Foucault wrote about that kind of mirror play in his 1966 book *The Order of Things*, and it opened a long line of interpretation. Another philosopher, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, described the mirror as an instrument that changes "me into others, and others into me." In this painting, you occupy the customer's place.

**The artist**

Édouard Manet painted this in 1882 and showed it at the Paris Salon, the official state exhibition, that same year. It is considered his last major work. He died the following year, in 1883. At the end of his career he was still doing what he had always done, which was to paint modern Paris as it actually looked. The first owner was the composer Emmanuel Chabrier, a close friend of Manet, who hung it above his piano.

**In this collection**

The painting came to The Courtauld through the collection of Samuel Courtauld, which also included a version of Manet's *Déjeuner sur l'Herbe*. It hangs in the LVMH Great Room alongside works by Degas, Monet and Renoir.

**What stays with you**

The crowd is glittering and loud, yet the woman at its centre is utterly still, and her eyes do not meet yours. Manet's final great picture places the viewer at the bar as the customer, and he keeps the barmaid's attention just out of reach.

title: Van Gogh’s iconic Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear
output:
# Audio Description: Van Gogh's *Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear*

**Orientation**

Stand about an arm's length from Van Gogh's iconic *Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear* and look at the green coat and the fur cap. From here you can see raised ridges of thick paint and the marks of the tool that laid them down. From across the room the surface flattens into colour, and that texture disappears.

**The Work**

Vincent van Gogh painted this in 1889. He faces us in a green overcoat and a blue cap trimmed with black fur. A white bandage covers one ear and wraps beneath his chin.

The cap is more than costume. He had just bought it to hold the heavy bandage in place and to keep out the winter cold. It records the hard conditions he was working under that January.

Behind him, three things share the wall. On the left is an open window. Beside it stands a canvas on an easel, bearing only a few marks that cannot be made out. On the right is a Japanese woodblock print, *Geishas in a Landscape*, made by Satō Torakiyo in the 1870s. Van Gogh owned that print. He collected hundreds of Japanese prints, and he copied this one into the painting.

Those prints taught him bold colour and new ways of arranging space, and he used both to modernise his style. Here they show in the strong, flat blocks of green, blue and orange that sit against one another without blending.

The ridges in front of you are impasto, paint applied so thickly that it holds the marks of the painting knife. Van Gogh used it to give the picture energy and passion. He had admired it in the work of Adolphe Monticelli, a painter whose heavily built-up canvases he praised in a letter to his brother Theo in 1888.

One detail is easy to miss. The bandage appears to cover his right ear, but the wound was to his left. He painted himself from a mirror, so the image is reversed. In a letter to Theo dated 17 January 1889, he mentioned a new self-portrait, which is believed to be this one.

**The Artist**

Van Gogh had left Paris for Arles, in the south of France, hoping to found the Studio of the South, a community of artists who would support one another. He rented four rooms in the Yellow House and invited Paul Gauguin, the French painter, to join him.

The plan fell apart within weeks. On the evening of 23 December 1888, Gauguin threatened to leave, and Van Gogh approached him with a razor. Later that night he cut off his own left ear and took it to a woman in Arles named Rachel. She was distressed, and she called the police, who arrested Van Gogh for lunacy.

This portrait was painted only weeks after that night. The shared studio he had worked toward was gone. He shows himself beside an easel, still dressed for work.

**The Emotional Reading**

The painting holds the wound and the work side by side. The bandage is framed by an easel and a print he loved, and the paint itself is laid on thickly and with force.

**In the Collection**

Samuel Courtauld bought the painting in 1928. It now stands at the centre of the Gallery's Impressionist and Post-Impressionist group, alongside Manet's *A Bar at the Folies-Bergère*, another of the collection's best-known paintings. It remains the self-portrait in which Van Gogh recorded his injury in paint.

title: Georges Seurat
output:
# Georges Seurat: *Young Woman Powdering Herself*
### The Courtauld Gallery, London

**Orientation**

You are standing before *Young Woman Powdering Herself* by Georges Seurat. Step close to the wall behind the seated woman, close enough to see the surface as separate marks rather than a smooth tone. From there, the shadows dissolve into tiny dots of distinct colour. Then step back several paces and watch them fuse into soft light and shade. Before you move on, look at the upper left corner, where a small vase of flowers sits in a frame on the wall. The most personal part of this painting is hidden there.

**The Work**

A full-figured young woman sits at a small dressing table and lifts a powder puff toward her face. She fills almost the entire lower canvas. The table looks almost toy-like against her, and her pose is stiff and upright, like a figure in a shop window.

The painting's method is its argument. Seurat built the modulation of light and shadow on the wall from small dots of pure, unmixed colour, set side by side in varying concentrations and intensity. Where the dots cluster densely and darkly, the wall falls into shadow. Where they thin and brighten, it glows. Seurat left the mixing to the viewer's eye instead of blending colours on his palette. This technique is called pointillism, and he developed it with Paul Signac, the younger French painter who became its leading advocate. That is why the surface looks granular up close and luminous from a distance. You are completing the colour yourself.

The model was Madeleine Knobloch, Seurat's mistress, who bore him two sons. That turns what looks like a modern scene of a woman at her toilette into a private portrait of the woman he lived with.

The corner holds something more personal still. A scan carried out by the Italian Institute of Optics revealed that the framed vase of flowers was originally a mirror. In it was a reflection of Seurat himself, at work at his easel, painting her. He covered it over. In doing so he erased what would have been the only self-portrait of the artist known to exist. The flowers you see now are a substitute for the painter's own face.

**The Artist**

Seurat was a French Neo-Impressionist, part of the generation that took the Impressionists' interest in light and tried to make it systematic, almost scientific. He painted this canvas between 1888 and 1890, near the end of a very short career. He died in March 1891, aged thirty-one. This is one of the few works in which his strict, theoretical method turns toward his own household, and then pulls back from it.

**The Emotional Reading**

Knowing about the hidden mirror changes how the painting feels. The cool, orderly dots record an intimate domestic moment, and the man who shared it chose to remove himself from the picture, leaving a vase where his face had been.

**In the Collection**

The painting belongs to the Samuel Courtauld Trust. It hangs in the Courtauld's Impressionist and Post-Impressionist galleries alongside Édouard Manet's *A Bar at the Folies-Bergère*, another image of a woman framed by a mirror, and Vincent van Gogh's *Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear*. Van Gogh painted himself unflinchingly. A few steps away, Seurat painted himself and then painted himself out.

# Audio Description: *Springtime* (1872)

**Orientation**

You're standing before *Springtime*, painted in 1872 by Claude Monet. Start a few steps back, where the whole canvas fits comfortably in your view. From there, the painting reads as a single scene. Then move closer to see how that scene is built up on the surface.

**The Work and the Artist**

*Springtime* is an 1872 painting by Claude Monet. Its title, a single word naming the season, tells you what the artist chose as his subject.

The title is shared by other works. The French painter Pierre Auguste Cot completed his own *Springtime* in 1873, just a year after this one. The American painter Wilbur Winfield Woodward also painted a *Springtime* later in the nineteenth century. So the work in front of you is the earliest of three nineteenth-century paintings that share this name. That small fact shows how often painters of the period returned to spring as a subject.

**The Emotional Reading**

The work rests on a plain idea: one season, set down by Monet in a single year, 1872.

title: The Death of Caesar
output:
**A note before the script:** The source material conflicts with the venue. The reference extract describes Vincenzo Camuccini's *The Death of Julius Caesar* (1806), which it places in the National Museum of Capodimonte in Naples, not the Walters. The Walters' venue sources don't mention a *Death of Caesar* at all. Before this stop is recorded, please confirm which work hangs at the Walters. If it is a different painting, this script will need new source material.

The script below uses only the Camuccini facts provided. The source gives no details about the canvas's size, colours or composition, so the orientation stays general rather than inventing what the listener will see.

---

**Audio Stop: The Death of Caesar**

Stand back from *The Death of Caesar* far enough to take in the whole canvas at once. This is a history painting, a picture meant to stage a turning point of the ancient world as a single scene. Its argument depends on seeing every figure together rather than one face at a time.

The painting shows the assassination of Julius Caesar, the Roman general and dictator stabbed by senators in 44 BC. Its painter was Vincenzo Camuccini, working in Rome. He finished this version in 1806, but it was not his first attempt.

Camuccini began with a cartoon in 1793. A cartoon is a full-scale preparatory drawing that maps out the composition before any paint is applied. That drawing won praise from the art critics of Rome. Three years later, in 1796, he completed a first painted version, and it was received less warmly. Camuccini destroyed it and started again from scratch. The canvas in front of you is the second painting, the product of roughly a decade of work on one subject.

The commission came from Frederick Hervey, the 4th Earl of Bristol, an English aristocrat and patron. Camuccini had already painted him a copy of Raphael's *Deposition*, the Renaissance master's scene of Christ's body being carried to the tomb. For a young painter, the leap from copying Raphael to inventing a grand Roman scene of his own was the step from apprentice to master. Camuccini staked that step on this painting.

The Earl died in 1803, three years before the painting was finished. His heirs refused to pay for it. In 1807 Camuccini sold it to Joachim Murat, the French cavalry commander Napoleon made King of Naples, and after Murat's fall it passed to the royal palace in Naples.

So the painting carries two kinds of loss. There is the first version Camuccini chose to destroy, and there is the patron who never lived to see the replacement. A picture about a murdered ruler was finished for a man already dead, and then sold to a king whose own reign would soon collapse.

## Draft Audio Stop: *Sappho and Alcaeus*

Stand close to *Sappho and Alcaeus*, about an arm's length away, and look at the curved marble bench where the women sit. At that distance, Greek letters carved into the seat backs come into focus. From across the room they read as nothing more than veining in the stone.

The painting shows a poetry recital on the Greek island of Lesbos around 600 BC. On the left, the poet Alcaeus plays a kithara, a large wooden lyre used for public performance. Across from him, Sappho leans forward on a marble desk and listens. She was the most celebrated woman poet of ancient Greece, famous for her lyrics of love and longing. Behind her sit young women from her circle. Beyond them, the Aegean Sea lies flat and blue past a grove of trees.

The painting is in oil, and its marble is its signature. The artist built the stone up in thin layers so that it seems to hold light and coolness, and visitors often sense its chill before they notice the figures. The carved letters on the bench are the names of women in Sappho's circle. The artist was signalling that this was archaeology, not fantasy.

The painter was Lawrence Alma-Tadema, a Dutch-born artist who made his career in London. He became one of the most successful painters of the Victorian era by staging ancient life with this kind of documentary detail. Critics in his lifetime praised his skill. Later critics dismissed him for turning antiquity into elegant Victorian drawing rooms. That tension is visible here, in a scene that is both carefully researched and deliberately serene.

The painting places a woman, not the male performer, at the centre of judgment. Alcaeus plays, but the scene is arranged around Sappho's attention. Within the Walters' collection, the work belongs with its nineteenth-century paintings, which often looked back to classical subjects.

What stays with the eye is the stillness. It is a moment of music rendered in stone and sea, with names carved into a bench by a painter who wanted the past to feel as solid as marble.

title: The Laughing Cavalier
output:
# The Laughing Cavalier, Frans Hals, 1624

Stand close to The Laughing Cavalier, near enough to see the right-hand sleeve clearly. From a distance, the embroidery looks laboriously finished, stitch by stitch. Up close, it dissolves into long, quick brushstrokes. Then step slowly to one side and back again. The man's eyes stay on you the whole way.

## The work

A man of twenty-six turns toward us, one hand on his hip. We know his age because Hals painted it into the canvas. At the top right is a Latin inscription: *aetatis suae 26, anno 1624*. It means "in his twenty-sixth year, in the year 1624," so he was born in 1597 or 1598.

His name was never recorded. Nineteenth-century titles cast him as a soldier, perhaps an officer in one of the part-time citizen militias. Dutch painters often portrayed these companies in groups, as Rembrandt later did in The Night Watch. But he could just as easily be a wealthy civilian. The art historian Pieter Biesboer has proposed the cloth merchant Tieleman Roosterman, whom Hals painted on another occasion.

The canvas measures about 83 by 67 centimetres, and much of it is given over to clothing. His silk costume was gorgeous and very expensive. Hals chose a low viewpoint and a turning pose, which push the embroidered sleeve and lace cuff toward us.

The embroidery carries a coded message. Bees, arrows, and flaming horns of plenty stand for the pleasures and pains of love. So do lovers' knots and tongues of fire. Beside them is an obelisk or pyramid, a sign of strength. There are also the winged cap and serpent-twined staff of Mercury, the Roman messenger god, signifying fortune. Whoever he was, this man wore his ambitions on his sleeve.

The painting's technique matters because it contradicts its subject. The costume would have taken months of skilled needlework. Hals rendered it in rapid, visible strokes. That speed is what makes the composition feel lively and spontaneous rather than stiff.

The famous title is misleading. Victorian audiences invented it after the painting was shown at the Bethnal Green Museum in East London in 1872. That exhibition was deliberately placed away from the fashionable West End to draw working-class visitors. The man is not laughing. He has an enigmatic smile, exaggerated by his upturned moustache.

Even a smile was unusual. Commissioned portraits rarely showed adults smiling until the late eighteenth century. Smiles appeared instead in "tronies," Dutch studies of expressive heads, and in genre paintings, which showed scenes of everyday life. The art historian Seymour Slive called this work "one of the most brilliant of all Baroque portraits."

The following eyes are no trick of special skill. The sitter looks straight out at the painter's position. Because the image is flat, that direct gaze meets you from whatever angle you stand.

## The artist

Frans Hals was a painter of the Dutch Golden Age, the period of Dutch prosperity and artistic flowering. He broke the rule against smiling sitters again and again, often painting broader grins than this one. He favoured informal poses that suggest movement and the impression of a moment caught. He also painted the militia group portraits that may explain this sitter's soldierly reputation.

This picture later reshaped how Hals was seen. At Bethnal Green it was a particular hit with the public and the critics alike. It played a considerable part in raising Hals's critical standing in England, and as prints spread it became one of the best-known old master paintings in Britain.

## Connections

The Marquess of Hertford bought it at a Paris auction in 1865, outbidding Baron James de Rothschild at more than six times the estimate. Today it hangs in the same collection as Fragonard's The Swing, the French painter's flirtatious garden scene, and both are among the most famous paintings in the world.

## What stays with you

The man is a stranger whose name was lost. Yet the painted grin and steady gaze make him feel like someone who has just recognised you. Four centuries on, he is still known by a laugh he never actually gave.

title: A Dance to the Music of Time
output:
# A Dance to the Music of Time: Audio Description

## Orientation

Stand a few paces back from *A Dance to the Music of Time*, square to the centre, so the ring of dancers and the sky above them fit in a single view. From there the painting reads as two linked bands of movement: four figures turning on the ground, and a sun-god's chariot sweeping across the dawn sky. Then step closer to the left edge. A small stone pillar topped with a carved head stands there, easily lost from a distance, and it holds one of the keys to what the picture means.

## The Work

Four figures hold hands and dance in a ring, facing outward. On the right, Time, a winged, naked old man, plays a lyre to set their rhythm. Above them it is early morning. Aurora, goddess of the dawn, flies ahead of the chariot of Apollo, the sun-god. Apollo is accompanied by the Hours, the goddesses of time's divisions, and he holds a ring representing the Zodiac, the circle of constellations that marks the passing year. The whole picture is built from circles: the dancers' ring, the Zodiac ring, and the endless turn of time.

Nicolas Poussin painted it between about 1634 and 1636 for Giulio Rospigliosi, a churchman who later became Pope Clement IX. According to Gian Pietro Bellori, an early writer on Poussin, Rospigliosi dictated the painting's detailed symbolism himself. In that reading, the four dancers form a cycle of human fortune. The figure at the back, seen mostly from behind, is Poverty. Poverty leads to Labour, Labour to Riches, and Riches to Pleasure or Luxury, which leads back to Poverty again.

The dancers can also be read as the Four Seasons. The art historian Anthony Blunt proposed that Autumn, the figure at the back, is unusually male. That view is now widely accepted, and the Wallace Collection identifies him as Bacchus, the god of wine. The idea follows a story in which Jupiter, king of the gods, gave mortals Bacchus and his wine to compensate them for their hard lives. André Félibien, Poussin's friend and biographer, explained the picture in much the same terms.

The scholar Malcolm Bull disagrees, at least about what was originally intended. He traces the imagery to Nonnus, a Late Greek poet, whose seasons Poussin seems to follow closely. In that reading, Spring is on the left with roses in her hair. Autumn is at the back, his hair cropped by the winds but wreathed with olive. Winter has bound hair and a shadowed face, and Summer is in front, dressed in white with ears of corn braided into her hair. In Bull's account, Bacchus appears instead in that small pillar at the left. It shows him in his double aspect, as both a young figure and an old one. Bull suggests Rospigliosi, an author with a taste for allegory, added the moral interpretation during or after the painting's completion. Another scholar, Ingamells, concluded that Poussin was not unduly concerned with naming each figure precisely.

The canvas shows signs of second thoughts. Poussin made several changes as he worked, known as pentimenti, which are traces of earlier painting later covered over. The largest was a second, bigger tree on the right, between Winter and Time, which he painted out. Removing it opened the gap through which the old man's music reaches the dancers.

The painting has also been damaged. A large L-shaped tear once ran right through the central group of dancers. It has been repaired and retouched, and the picture is otherwise in generally good condition. The ring held together, though the canvas beneath it once split.

The painting's famous title is relatively recent. It first appears in a Wallace Collection catalogue of 1913. Earlier titles referred to the Four Seasons, and at an 1845 sale it was called *The Dance of the Seasons, or the Image of Human Life*. The 1913 title later gave its name to Anthony Powell's novel cycle. In the opening pages of the first book, the narrator recalls Poussin's Seasons, "hand in hand and facing outward," and is led to thoughts of mortality.

## The Artist

Poussin made this work as a commission from a powerful patron who wanted to shape its meaning himself. The painting sits between the two men's intentions: Rospigliosi's moral allegory and Poussin's own response to ancient poetry. Félibien, who knew Poussin personally, accepted the patron's reading. Modern scholars are still arguing over how much of it the painter shared.

## What You Notice

Because the dancers face outward, none of them looks at the others, and none can see who leads. Time keeps playing while the sun rises overhead, and the dance continues regardless of who is rich or poor at any given turn.

title: Madame de Pompadour
output:
# Madame de Pompadour: Audio Description

**Orientation**

Stand a few paces back from *Madame de Pompadour*, square to the canvas, so the whole portrait fills your view at once. That distance matches how the painting was first meant to be seen: on public display at the Château de Versailles, the royal palace outside Paris, where courtiers would have taken it in as a single image of the sitter. Up close you see brushwork. From here you see the portrait as a finished statement.

**The Work**

This is a portrait of Madame de Pompadour, painted in oil on canvas in 1759. Its importance comes from where it falls in a sequence. François Boucher painted Madame de Pompadour seven times, and this is the seventh and last. Whatever he had worked out about her face, her bearing and her presentation over the six earlier portraits, this canvas is where that long effort ends.

Oil on canvas suited that purpose. It is a medium that can be built up and revised in layers, and Boucher was revising one sitter across an entire series. Each new portrait was a chance to refine the image, and this is the version he left as his final word.

The painting was not made for a private room. It was first exhibited at Versailles, the centre of court life, so it was shown where the sitter's image carried the most weight. Afterward it passed to her brother. A portrait displayed before the court became a family possession.

**The Artist**

François Boucher was a painter of the French Rococo, the light, ornamental style that dominated eighteenth-century French art and decoration. By 1759 he had returned to this one sitter again and again. Few painters of the period are linked so closely to a single patron and subject. This canvas marks the end of that working relationship on canvas. After this, there would be no eighth portrait.

**The Emotional Reading**

The sense of finality is part of what you are seeing. You are looking at the last time Boucher painted Madame de Pompadour, the point where seven attempts to capture one woman came to rest.

title: Officer and Laughing Girl
output:
# Officer and Laughing Girl, by Johannes Vermeer

**Orientation**

Stand directly in front of *Officer and Laughing Girl*, close enough that the canvas fills your view, then take one step to the left, toward the side where the painted window lets in light. From here, the officer's dark shape in the foreground looms between you and the woman, as if you are standing just behind his shoulder. The light that falls on her face reaches you across his silhouette. Up close, you can also make out the map on the back wall, which Vermeer painted precisely enough that scholars can identify its exact edition.

**The Work**

This is an oil painting on canvas made around 1657, and it is small: about fifty by forty-six centimetres. Vermeer packs a whole drama into that space. A young woman in a yellow bodice sits at a table, smiling, a wine glass in her hand. Opposite her, a cavalier in a red coat and a broad black hat sits with his back half-turned to us.

The officer's size is the painting's central trick. He is much larger than the woman, pushed into the immediate foreground. This device is called repoussoir, from the French for "to push back." A large dark form placed up front makes everything behind it seem to recede, deepening the room. Caravaggio, the Italian painter famous for dramatic, theatrical lighting, used it often, and Vermeer probably learned it from Caravaggio's imitators. Art historians believe a painting by Gerard van Honthorst inspired this composition. Some also suggest Vermeer used a camera obscura, a darkened box with a lens that projects an image of a scene, to work out the steep perspective between the two figures.

The clothing tells us about these people. The officer's hat is beaver pelt, weather-resistant and costly. The pelts were imported from the New World, probably from New Netherland, today's eastern United States, then controlled by the Dutch West India Company, a trading company with colonial powers. His black sash marks his rank. The woman's yellow bodice, with its braided trim, was an everyday garment called a schort. A blue apron, mostly lost in the shadow of the table, was worn because blue hid stains. Some historians read this as a sign that he has dropped in unannounced during her morning chores. Her glass is the kind used for white wine, and wine cost more than beer, so the glass signals means.

The map behind them shows Holland and West Friesland, a map by Willem Blaeu and Balthasar Florisz. van Berckenrode. Vermeer must have owned it, because it appears in three of his paintings. The scholar Peter van der Krogt pointed out that Vermeer painted it so faithfully, down to its mounting on linen and wooden rods, that it can be identified as Blaeu's 1621 map.

X-ray photographs reveal what Vermeer gave up along the way. He first planned a large white collar on the woman, which would have covered much of her yellow dress. He painted it out. He also extended her cap to cover all her hair, so nothing competes with her face and her expression.

What that expression means is still argued over. Many art historians see an innocent, honourable courtship. Others read her open hand and her smile as a discreet willingness to go further. The painting does not settle it.

**The Artist**

Johannes Vermeer was a Dutch painter of the seventeenth century, and this canvas already holds the elements that define his work. There is a woman in yellow, daylight entering from an open window on the left, and a map on the wall. Each recurs in other paintings. What sets this one apart is the man seated at the table with her. The woman resembles Vermeer's wife, Catharina Bolnes, who is believed to have posed for many of his paintings. So the face he cleared of collar and hair may have been the one he knew best.

**In the Collection**

This is one of the Frick's three Vermeers, alongside *Girl Interrupted at Her Music* and *Mistress and Maid*. It recently inspired new paintings by Kent Monkman, a contemporary Canadian artist who examines European art from an Indigenous perspective. Monkman's work looks at how pictures like this one quietly recorded global trade and colonization, starting with the officer's beaver hat.

**The Emotional Reading**

Because the officer blocks part of our view, we watch the woman's laughter much as he does, from the shadow and at an angle. The light on her face was earned by removing the collar and covering the hair, and it falls just beyond our reach.

title: Portrait of Sir Thomas More
output:
# Portrait of Sir Thomas More

Stand close to Holbein's **Portrait of Sir Thomas More**, near enough to see the sitter's hands, and look first at the upper right corner of the panel. From a distance, that corner reads as background. Up close, a thin cord comes into focus, tied in a loose Franciscan knot. Lower down, on More's left index finger, a wedding ring set with a stone appears. These details are small and easy to miss, yet they carry much of the portrait's meaning.

**The painting**

Hans Holbein the Younger painted this portrait in 1527, in oil on an oak panel. The hard, close-grained wood gave him a smooth surface for the fine detail he is known for. That surface lets you separate the textures of More's clothing: the soft fur lining of his coat, the deep red velvet of his sleeves, and the cooler sheen of black satin. More sits in three-quarter view, turned toward your right, holding a book. The book marks him as a humanist, one of the scholars of the period who revived the study of classical learning.

Across his chest hangs a heavy gold chain called the Collar of Esses, a livery chain made of linked S-shaped forms and hung with a Tudor rose, the emblem of the English royal house. It declares loyalty to the king and high office. More was then a knight and a powerful speaker in the English Parliament.

The portrait sets two kinds of commitment side by side. The chain stands for public duty to the crown. The cord in the corner, knotted in the manner of the Franciscans, the religious order devoted to poverty, points to More's private spiritual convictions. The ring adds a third commitment, to his marriage. Holbein puts worldly power at the centre and quiet signs of faith at the edges.

A related drawing in chalk with bodycolour, meaning opaque watercolour, survives in the Royal Collection in Britain, though scholars think it was probably not a direct study for this panel. A copy in London's National Portrait Gallery was probably painted in Italy or Austria in the early seventeenth century, which shows how widely this image of More was wanted long after his lifetime.

**The artist**

Holbein was a German painter and printmaker who arrived in London in 1526. He came with a recommendation from Desiderius Erasmus, the Dutch humanist scholar and the most famous intellectual in Europe, who urged him to seek out More. This portrait is part of the result of that introduction. Holbein also painted a large group portrait of More's family, but that painting is now lost. Only drawings, most of them also in the Royal Collection, and later copies record it, which makes this panel one of the few surviving paintings from Holbein's first years in England.

**What you notice**

More's direct, alert face sits above all this splendour, and the effect is of a man fully at ease in office yet signalling, in the margins, loyalties beyond it. In a museum currently exploring Gainsborough's portraits and the language of fashion, this panel shows that two and a half centuries earlier, clothing and jewellery were already a portrait's way of stating who a person was and to whom he answered.

The knot in the corner is loose, and the chain is heavy.

title: Portrait of Comtesse d'Haussonville

# Portrait of Comtesse d'Haussonville
### Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, 1845

**Orientation**

Begin a few steps back from *Portrait of Comtesse d'Haussonville*, where the woman, the dresser and the mirror read as one cool field of pale blue, grey and gold. Then move close and look past her shoulder into the mirror. There you'll find what the front view hides: the back of her head, with a crimson ribbon tied into her parted hair. It is the only strong warm note in the painting, and Ingres placed it where you can see it only in reflection.

**The Work**

Louise de Broglie, the Comtesse d'Haussonville, was twenty-seven when Ingres painted her in oil on canvas. She faces you fully, with a demure expression. Her left index finger is raised coyly to her mouth. Her right arm curls across her body, sinuous and longer than any real arm could be.

That arm is deliberate. Ingres stretched the anatomy to make the line of the body flow, choosing grace of contour over accuracy. The finger and the arm are the core of the composition. They appear in every version he attempted.

The mirror is a device he had used once before, in his 1814 *Portrait of Madame de Senonnes*, where a sitter is also doubled by a glass behind her. Here it shows you two views of the same woman at once.

On the dresser in front of the mirror are her writing materials, along with pots, flowers and a lavishly decorated oriental vase. The writing materials suit the sitter. Highly educated, she later became an essayist and biographer, and wrote historical romances based on the lives of figures including Lord Byron, the English Romantic poet.

Look at the satin of her dress. It is heavily folded, cold and grey-blue, and Ingres painted it in the same hue as her eyes. The dress and the gaze are tied together by a single colour.

This canvas cost years of effort. Two or three years earlier, Ingres made a black chalk drawing of her and began a first oil version. In that version the pose was reversed and there was no mirror. He worked slowly and demanded long sittings, and she found them tedious. At one point she complained that "for the last nine days Ingres has been painting on one of the hands." Then she became pregnant with her third child and could no longer pose. That 1842 painting was abandoned and remains unfinished. The version in front of you is the second attempt, signed and dated by Ingres at the lower left.

Her family was delighted with it. A visitor named Monsieur Thiers came to see it with the sitter and teased her more than once: "M. Ingres must be in love with you to have painted you that way."

In 1846 the painting was shown in Paris alongside two of Ingres's images of women, the *Grande Odalisque* and *Odalisque with Slave*. The poet Charles Baudelaire praised all three for their "voluptuousness," meaning their sensual richness. Afterwards he called Ingres the quintessential painter of women. Critics have often compared the intensity of her gaze to Ingres's later *Portrait of Madame Moitessier*.

**The Artist**

By 1845 Ingres was at the height of his fame and much in demand as a portraitist. He resented it. His ambition was history painting: large scenes from myth and the past, which he considered the highest form of art. To his frustration, those scenes paid far less than portraits. That year he agreed to only two portrait commissions, this one and the *Portrait of Baronne de Rothschild*.

Even after the family's praise, he insisted he had failed. "I do not feel that I have conveyed all the graces of that charming model," he wrote. The irony is that his portraits are what he is best known for today, and this is one of them.

**The Emotional Reading**

The painting holds two things in tension. The surface is cool, with icy satin and a pale, steady gaze. Yet the gesture is intimate, a finger hovering at her lips. Behind her, the small red ribbon in the mirror is the one detail Ingres seems to have kept for those who look closely.
